thread.title_full: Illinois Tollway board votes unanimously to approve toll rate hike - NewsBreak

author: Winnie Dortch
title: Illinois Tollway board votes unanimously to approve toll rate hike - NewsBreak
text:
By Winnie Dortch Michael Johnson Alonzo Small Dana Rebik ,
7 hours ago
LAKE FOREST, Ill. ( WGN ) — The Illinois Tollway Authority Board has approved the largest toll rate increase in state history, an increase the board says is necessary to fund a major capital investment program that will go toward infrastructure projects.
The rate hike, which will begin in January, was approved Wednesday by a unanimous 8-0 vote, despite the measure being opposed by some commuters and critics.
The board says that since the tollway is a user-funded system that receives no federal or state tax dollars, the rate hike is necessary to be the primary source of funds for the "Driving Connections" capital investment program, which will allocate $26.5 billion over 15 years for projects like road and bridge repairs and congestion relief.
"This represents the first rate increase in more than 15 years and ensures rates remain below the national average," the board said in a news release.
How much will rates increase? Beginning January 1, passenger vehicles will see a 45-cent per-toll increase, while commercial vehicles will face a 30% hike.
For example, if drivers hit three tolls each way on their commute, they could pay nearly $500 more per year. The rates would then be adjusted every other year based on inflation.
In 2025, Illinois lawmakers redirected $1.1 billion from the state road fund in order to bail out the Regional Transit Authority, which oversees CTA, Metra and Pace, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker brokered a deal to authorize the tollway to raise rates.
Labor groups have supported the measure to increase toll rates.
"This program invests in Illinois workers by funding construction projects that create opportunities for skilled tradespeople, suppliers and small businesses," Devereaux Johnson of the Indiana, Illinois, Iowa Foundation for Fair Contracting (III FFC) , said on July 13.
The Illinois Tollway board said Wednesday's vote was the culmination of a more than two-year process, during which it hosted 13 public hearings across 12 counties served by the tollway and gathered more than 13,000 comments, claiming customers said affordability, well-maintained roads and fewer traffic delays were among their priorities.
"We listened, we planned, and now we have a responsibility to deliver," Illinois Tollway Executive Director Cassaundra Rouse said in the release. "Nearly 1.7 million drivers rely on this system every day, and our responsibility extends well beyond the next construction season.
"We know where congestion is growing, and we know how our infrastructure ages. 'Driving Connections' gives us a responsible path to meet those needs and keep northern Illinois moving for the next generation."
Commuters raise concerns Still, despite the board's unanimous vote and insistence that the rate hike is necessary, critics and commuters raised concerns in previous weeks and months regarding the financial burden on residents and the speed of the legislative process.
Over the summer, drivers expressed their concerns at more than a dozen public hearings on the issue. Grayslake driver Allan Conrad told WGN-TV on Tuesday that it's a lot for a normal working person to absorb.
"When they drive the tollway every day to and from, it adds up, along with the gas prices and taxes," Conrad said.
The thought of spending more money also alarmed one Winfield driver who commutes from I-294 to I-94 northbound.
"It's really an expense for me," she said.
Bryce Hill, senior director of fiscal and economic analysis at the Illinois Policy Institute , said prior to Wednesday's vote that the process leading up to it was rushed.
"There was plenty of time to be able to vet this," Hill said. "Instead, we have this political and highly rushed process that we're seeing now."
At a series of public hearings, WGN cameras did capture overwhelming support from union workers for the toll hike. Still, a Freedom of Information Act request showed that public online comments leaned the other way.
"We got nearly 14,000 responses back from the tollway that they had collected, and we found that 76% of the people who had responded, nearly 10,000, were opposed," Hill said.
Added Conrad: "It seems like it's very typical Illinois politics where the regular person or citizen doesn't have a say, and you don't even get a chance to say, because they do a lot of these back-door deals."
But not all commuters opposed the rate increase, including one who spoke ahead of Wednesday's vote.
"Today I am here to express my strong support for the Illinois Tollway's 'Driving Connections' capital program, including the investment to rehabilitate roadways, improve infrastructure and reduce congestion," Berwyn resident Emily Kraiem said.
"As our communities continue to grow, these investments will help ensure that families like mine continue to reach life's most important moments safely and efficiently."
